title: How the Mafia Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how the Mafia works: the five Italian mafia groups (Sicilian Mafia, Camorra, 'Ndrangheta, Sacra Corona Unita, and Cosa Nostra in America), the hierarchy (boss/don, underboss, capos, soldiers, associates, consigliere), the five New York families and their naming, the induction ceremony and made-man requirements, the Commission, mob revenue through extortion, labor unions and pensions, Sicilian feudal roots and the Maxi Trial, the American mafia's history including Vegas, the Kennedy connections, and how the RICO Act is used against organized crime. The episode closes with listener mail about a falling-airplane story and an on-air sign-off.

segments.title: Intro and naming the Mafia groups
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic, clarify that 'the mafia' refers to Italian organized crime, and list the five Italian mafia groups: Sicilian Mafia, Camorra, Calabrian mafia, Sacra Corona Unita, and Cosa Nostra in America. They define Cosa Nostra and the code of silence (omerta).

segments.title: Mafia hierarchy and ranks
segments.summary: Explanation of the family structure: families, bosses (dons), underbosses, capos, soldiers, associates, and made men. Hosts compare the hierarchy to corporate management.

segments.title: The consigliere
segments.summary: The consigliere is described as an outside advisor and tiebreaker, not a family member, and is elected in theory but often appointed by the boss in practice. Movie examples from The Godfather are discussed.

segments.title: Naming the New York families
segments.summary: There is no single head of the mafia; a commission acts as a governing body. The five New York families got their names from Joe Valachi's 1963 Senate subcommittee testimony, and families were often named after their powerful bosses. Examples of family name changes such as the Profaci family becoming the Colombo family are given.

segments.title: Becoming a made man and the induction ceremony
segments.summary: Requirements for membership include Italian heritage (ideally both parents) and proven work. The induction ceremony involves oaths, burning a holy card, a blood-drawn trigger finger pledge, a godfather guide, and a rumored murder requirement. Candidates must be approved by the Commission.

segments.title: The Commission and Lucky Luciano
segments.summary: The Commission was formed in the 1920s and 1930s amid violent competition during Prohibition to register members and control murders. Lucky Luciano is credited with creating it and setting up the five families. The Commission also weeded out members with feuds and reduced anonymity.

segments.title: How the mafia makes money: extortion and labor unions
segments.summary: Mob income comes from extortion and protection fees, illegal goods and services, hijacking, and infiltrating labor unions. Jimmy Hoffa and the Teamsters pension fund are discussed, including how the pension was used to underwrite Las Vegas casinos.

segments.title: Feudal roots of the Sicilian mafia and the Maxi Trial
segments.summary: The mafia is linked to Sicily's feudal system, where landowners extracted tribute and used violence. After Mussolini's crackdown and the postwar period, the Cupola formed. The 1980s Maxi Trial convicted many mobsters, but many were acquitted or later freed on appeal, and Italy sent troops to Sicily.

segments.title: American mafia history: New Orleans, New York, Appalachian meeting
segments.summary: Early Italian mafia incident in New Orleans in the 1890s, where a lynch mob killed sixteen. New York's mafia growth during Prohibition, boss killings, and the 1957 Appalachian meeting raided by a state trooper, which exposed the mafia publicly.

segments.title: Kennedy family and mafia connections
segments.summary: Discussion of alleged mafia ties to the Kennedy family: Joe Kennedy's alleged bootlegging, Lucky Luciano and Meyer Lansky, Lee Harvey Oswald, the Bay of Pigs, Robert Kennedy's pursuit of the mob, and Sam Giancana's alleged links to JFK and Marilyn Monroe. These are presented as allegations.

segments.title: Las Vegas, the mob, and movies
segments.summary: Mob involvement in early Las Vegas casinos, with Jewish mobsters and Italian mob partnerships funded through union pensions. Hosts discuss movies including Casino and Goodfellas and note Vegas has been cleaner since the 1970s.

segments.title: Fighting the mafia: RICO Act and undercover work
segments.summary: The RICO Act of 1970 allows prosecution of an entire criminal enterprise and its boss for racketeering, with at least two felonies in a fifteen-year period. Undercover work, such as Joe Pistone's infiltration, is also discussed. Hosts note RICO is now used mostly against corporations.

segments.title: Wrap-up and reading suggestions
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up, suggest further reading on the How Stuff Works site, and recommend mafia films.

segments.title: Listener mail: falling airplane story
segments.summary: Hosts read a listener story about a near-crash landing at Shannon Airport in Ireland in 2007 and discuss the flight, followed by a call for mafia stories by email.
